structured_output.summary: Nothing can be reviewed yet: hypothesis.tsv, results.tsv, predictions.tsv and the notebook are all empty. No conclusions exist, so none rests on a single run, sits within noise, or is contradicted by results. The real risk is the opposite: the loop may start optimizing before it has a baseline, a noise estimate, or any Lvl1 claims to test. The critiques below cover what to set up first, the noise and selection traps built into the 3-seed / 0.753 rule, and rule pitfalls likely to invalidate early 'wins': flip TTA in borrowed recipes, data-dependent init in build, recompiles during eval, and timing differences between the SXM experiment GPU and the PCIe judging GPU.

critiques.issue: There are no Lvl1 claims. Without them, every experiment is a blind tweak and no verdict can sharpen anything. The objective (time at a fixed accuracy) naturally splits into three independent factors, and none is written down.
critiques.suggestion: Seed the tree with three Lvl1 hypotheses before experimenting. H1: time is driven by sample efficiency, meaning how many steps or epochs are needed to reach 75.3% (architecture, optimizer, schedule, label smoothing, augmentation). H2: time is driven by per-step throughput (bf16/channels_last, torch.compile, batch size, GPU-resident data, kernel fusion). H3: time is driven by fixed overhead in prepare and startup (moving data to the GPU, decoding, data-dependent init, first-iteration costs). Give each a Lvl3 prediction with a number in it, e.g. 'bf16 + channels_last cuts epoch time by at least 30% with no change in accuracy.'

critiques.issue: There is no reference point. You can't judge whether a change helps without the template's time and accuracy, plus a breakdown of where time goes.
critiques.suggestion: Run 1 should be the unmodified template, run as-is. Record prepare time and train time separately, and per-epoch time, so the H1, H2 and H3 shares can be read off directly rather than guessed.

critiques.target: Noise model (no estimate of seed-to-seed or run-to-run variance)
critiques.issue: With 3 seeds, the SE of the mean accuracy is std/√3. If the per-seed std is around 0.3–0.4 pp, the 0.3 pp margin (0.753 vs 0.75) is only about 1.3–1.7 SE. Time also varies from run to run (GPU clocks, compile caches, CPU contention on 4 cores). Any accuracy delta under about 0.3 pp or time delta under a few percent can't be read until this is measured.
critiques.suggestion: Early on, run the same config twice, or read the per-seed values if they're logged, to estimate the per-seed accuracy std and the run-to-run time std. Write down a minimum detectable effect, and mark any verdict whose delta falls inside it as E~ rather than E+ or E-.

critiques.issue: The loop will keep the fastest config that clears 0.753 on 3 fixed seeds. Choosing the minimum-time config among many that only just pass is a winner's curse: its true 40-seed mean is biased downward and may fall below 75%. Because the seeds are fixed (0, 1, 2), the recipe can also end up tuned to those particular seeds.
critiques.suggestion: Treat any frontier result below about 0.756 as provisional. Before accepting it as the incumbent, re-run with a different seed offset in a local test harness, or run more seeds outside the official command. Prefer trading a little speed for 0.5 pp or more of headroom.

critiques.target: Never-tried direction: published fast CIFAR recipes (airbench-style)
critiques.issue: The obvious prior is to adapt known fast CIFAR-10 recipes (airbench / hlb-CIFAR10: patch-whitening first layer, Lookahead/EMA, label smoothing, very high LR with a short schedule, GPU-side random crop/flip). But those reported accuracies include horizontal-flip TTA, which this task forbids, and the whitening init reads training data.
critiques.suggestion: Write an Lvl2 under H1 for this. Its Lvl3 prediction should explicitly budget the roughly 0.3–0.6 pp lost to no TTA. Compute any whitening or data-dependent init inside prepare (timed), not in build. Expect CIFAR-100 at 75% to need a wider or deeper net, or more epochs, than airbench94/96 uses.

critiques.target: Rule risk: eval with torch.compile and any batch size B from 1 to 1024
critiques.issue: A compiled eval path with static shapes can recompile for each new B. That could break the 5 s eval limit or the requirement to return finite [B,100] logits for every B. A training-time win would then still produce an invalid (incomplete) run.
critiques.suggestion: Either evaluate in eager mode or with mark_dynamic, or pad inputs to fixed buckets and warm those up in build using synthetic data. Add a local check over B ∈ {1, 7, 513, 1024} before trusting any compiled config.

critiques.target: Rule risk: state reset and leakage between trials
critiques.issue: EMA buffers, BN running stats, optimizer state, Lookahead copies, cached whitening matrices and RNGs all have to be reset in prepare. Anything cached in build from real data is a violation. A config that leaks state makes trials 2 and 3 look better and quietly inflates the mean.
critiques.suggestion: Add a Lvl3 sanity prediction: accuracy for seed 0 should be statistically indistinguishable from seeds 1 and 2, with no upward trend in trial order. Audit prepare whenever a new stateful component is added.

critiques.issue: With 4 pinned cores, any CPU-side augmentation or DataLoader pipeline will probably bottleneck an A100 at the small model sizes speedruns use. Nothing is in place to detect this.
critiques.suggestion: Under H2, predict that moving the full uint8 dataset to the GPU once in prepare, and doing crop/flip/cutout on the GPU, reduces epoch time by a measurable amount. Check for a CPU bottleneck by comparing GPU utilization, or step time against a synthetic-data step time.

critiques.target: Hardware mismatch: A100 SXM experiments, A100 PCIe judging
critiques.issue: PCIe A100s have a lower power limit (300 W vs 400 W) and can clock lower under sustained load. Gains from tuning for compute-bound kernels on SXM may shrink on PCIe, and absolute times will differ.
critiques.suggestion: Treat absolute times as SXM-specific and prefer changes that cut work (fewer epochs, fewer FLOPs) over ones that only exploit SXM headroom. Note this as a known gap between the local metric and the official judgment.

critiques.issue: Compiling in build is untimed. But compiling on synthetic shapes that differ from real training shapes (last partial batch, a change of resolution partway through a progressive-resize schedule) causes recompiles inside train, which are timed and invisible unless logged.
critiques.suggestion: Use drop_last or fixed batch shapes, and warm up every shape the schedule will use in build. Log recompile events (TORCH_LOGS=recompiles) during a prepare+train run to confirm there are zero.
